name: chain-of-responsibility
intent: Decouple a request sender from any particular receiver by composing an ordered set of handlers; each link explicitly chooses to handle and stop, to forward, or (in a middleware-style variant) to run around the successor.
problem: Several components may be able to respond to the same request, but the responsible component and the required order vary by route, deployment, or runtime policy. Hard-coding those checks in one dispatcher or duplicating them across entry points makes ordering, short-circuiting, and the unhandled outcome implicit and fragile.
context: Request-processing paths where a request may be offered to potential receivers - protocol middleware, GUI event bubbling, validation and authorisation stages, log/exception handlers, approval and escalation levels - and composition policy decides membership and order. Distinguish first-handler-wins from middleware/interceptor chains that wrap a successor and may run on the response path; in either case, every branch must define handle, forward, or terminal behavior.
benefits: Sender and receiver are decoupled: the caller submits to the chain's entry point and never names a concrete handler, so handlers are added, removed or reordered without touching the caller.
Each link is a small, independently testable unit with one responsibility (authentication, validation, caching, formatting), instead of a monolithic processing method.
Ordering becomes an explicit, declarative artifact - registration order, a MIDDLEWARE list, an app.use stack, a filter list - that a deployment can vary per route or per environment.
Open/closed: new cross-cutting steps plug into the composition rather than editing the dispatcher, so the modification surface stays small.
One structure covers both documented readings: first-handler-wins (the classic request is consumed) and every-handler-runs-with-short-circuit (middleware pipelines that wrap the rest of the chain).
tradeoffs: No guarantee of handling: if the chain has no terminal handler the request can fall off the end and be ignored silently.

Handler order is a policy that lives in configuration rather than in the call graph, so a wrong order changes behaviour without a compile error (authorisation registered after the handler it guards, a cache that swallows requests).
Dispatch is indirection: the code that produced a result is data, not a call site, which makes stack traces and debugging less direct.
Every hop costs a dispatch - virtual call, delegate invocation, framework hook - and per-request handler objects add allocation on a hot path.
A chain that can be rewired at runtime invalidates assumptions about a handler's successor, and exhaustive testing of order permutations is combinatorially expensive.
Precedence can be ambiguous: with the 'several handlers may also act' reading, the effect depends on how far the request travels, and a handler that does not forward silently skips every later stage.

participants.responsibility: Declares the request-handling operation and, in the classic form, the successor reference; every link implements the same contract so the sender stays unaware of concrete handlers.
Decides for the request it receives whether to handle it (and stop) or forward it to its successor; owns the work it does, e.g. authentication, validation, caching, translation.
Guarantees a defined outcome for requests nobody claimed; without it a request can be dropped silently at the end of the chain.
Submits the request to the chain - usually to its first link - and stays decoupled from which handler ultimately answers it.
Assembles the ordered chain from configuration or registration (successor links, middleware list, filter registration, ServiceBuilder) and therefore fixes handler order and membership.

use_cases: HTTP request pipelines: authentication, CORS, compression, rate limiting and routing registered as an ordered middleware stack (Express, ASP.NET Core, Django, Rack, Ktor, NestJS).
GUI and DOM event propagation: a click or help event bubbles from the focused widget up through panels to the window until an element can act on it.
Approval and escalation workflows: a purchase request is offered to the team lead, then the department head, then the CFO, each with its own authority limit.

Logging and exception handling: a record is offered to handlers by severity (console, file, alerting) until one accepts it, and error pages are rendered by the first handler that recognises the exception.
Input validation and sanitisation stages before a command is executed, where the first stage that rejects short-circuits the rest.
Plugin or command dispatch: a request carries a command id and the first plugin able to process that id executes it.
Event-sourcing command pipelines: a command object travels a chain of handlers (validation, authorisation, deduplication, snapshot policy) before being committed to the event store.
Message-queue processing chains: a message from a broker passes through consumer-side handlers (deserialisation, schema validation, idempotency check, routing) before reaching the business handler.

ML inference preprocessing pipelines: an input tensor is passed through a chain of preprocessing stages (normalisation, augmentation, feature extraction) before reaching the model; each stage may short-circuit on invalid input.

Web Application Firewall (WAF) and security filter chains: incoming requests traverse rule-based filters (SQL injection detection, CSRF token validation, IP allow/deny list, rate limiting) where each filter decides to block, sanitise, or pass the request.

Dynamic plugin discovery and dispatch: an editor plugin host scans installed packages and chains their handlers, each advertising a supported file type or action, so the first compatible plugin processes the user action.
Feature-flag evaluation chains: a request for a flag value travels through handlers (user targeting, percentage roll-out, environment override, default fallback) until a concrete value is returned.
Content negotiation pipelines: an HTTP request passes through content-type handlers (JSON, XML, Protobuf) until one matches the Accept header and can serialise the response.

Retry and circuit-breaker pipelines: a failed outbound call is offered to a retry handler that re-queues it, then a circuit-breaker handler that trips on repeated failures, before a dead-letter handler records the exhaustion of recovery options.

Jakarta Servlet FilterChain: each configured Filter examines a request and either calls chain.doFilter(request, response) to reach the next filter/resource or writes a response to block it, with deployment order acting as policy.

Express 5 app.use middleware: functions receive req, res, and next; they can end the response, call next() to continue, or pass errors to next(err), so a missing terminal response or next() leaves the request unresolved.

Django's MIDDLEWARE list: each factory receives get_response for the next layer, can short-circuit before the view, and runs response work while unwinding the ordered stack; the documented order is part of the contract.

Spring Security FilterChainProxy: the servlet container delegates to FilterChainProxy, which selects the first SecurityFilterChain whose RequestMatcher matches and runs only that chain's ordered filters (authentication before authorization), so a custom filter added with addFilterAfter changes policy without touching the dispatcher.

Netty ChannelPipeline: each Channel owns a pipeline of ChannelHandlers; inbound events propagate handler-to-handler only when the current handler calls the matching ChannelHandlerContext fire method, so a decoder that forgets to fire channelRead silently stalls every later handler, and only @Sharable handlers may be shared across pipelines.
avoid_when: Exactly one handler is known statically - a direct method call, or a Strategy selected once, is simpler and cheaper than an indirect chain.
Every stage must always run and transform a value - use Pipe and Filter or a deliberate Decorator/Pipeline, not a handle-or-forward chain whose links may stop early.
The branch is a data-driven routing decision over a small closed set of cases - a switch or lookup table makes the exhaustive alternatives clearer than a chain of objects.

The runtime already owns the request pipeline (Jakarta FilterChain, ASP.NET Core middleware, Rack, Ktor or Express) - register the component in that chain instead of rebuilding Chain-of-Responsibility roles around it.

Order correctness cannot be verified and a skipped step is a security or consistency hole - prefer an explicit orchestrator (Template Method or Command Processor) whose call order is visible and testable.
The requirement is fan-out to every independent observer rather than selection or ordered short-circuiting - use Observer or publish/subscribe so one consumer cannot accidentally suppress the others.

The requirement is only before/after advice around one known target and no handler-selection policy - use an Interceptor or Decorator, which makes the wrapped target and continuation contract explicit.
anti_patterns: Chain with no terminal handler: requests nobody claims disappear; the default outcome must be an explicit handler or a documented, logged failure.
Handlers used as decorators - every link does work and unconditionally forwards - so the request is processed N times and the stop/pass contract is lost.
A globally mutable chain that is rebuilt per request or rewired from several threads, producing order-dependent, non-reproducible behaviour.
Using a chain where the decision has exactly one right answer at build time (a switch over a closed enum); the indirection hides the branch without adding flexibility.

Silent short-circuit as a security control: an authorisation handler registered after the handler it guards, or one that only forwards on the happy path, lets untrusted work run without the required decision.

Async handler not awaiting next(): the successor call is issued without await, so the function returns before downstream processing and the request appears complete with an incomplete response; await the successor or return its promise.
Mutable shared state between requests: a handler instance carries per-request state in instance fields shared across concurrent requests, producing data leakage or race-condition bugs.
Circular chain: two or more handlers reference each other as successor, creating an infinite forwarding loop that hangs or stack-overflows at runtime.
Premature optimization — skipping the terminal handler: the developer wires the chain without a default fallback to save a handler slot, silently dropping requests that fall off the end.
Mixing sync and async handlers in a chain without a unified signature: callers cannot predict whether to await or invoke synchronously, leading to unhandled promises or deadlocks in production.

Chains built inside handlers: handler constructors or handle() methods assemble sub-chains, tightly coupling the handler to its successor topology and making unit testing impossible without instantiating the full chain.
design_principles: Single responsibility: each handler owns exactly one request-processing concern.
Open/closed principle: new handlers extend the composition instead of editing the dispatcher.
Loose coupling and information hiding: the sender knows only the chain's entry point, a handler knows only its successor.
Composition over inheritance: successors are wired by composition - a link, a list, a registration - not by subclassing the chain.
Explicit policy: handler order is declared configuration, validated at startup, not implied by scattered call sites.
Fail-safe defaults: an unhandled request must be an explicit, observable outcome.
best_practices: Terminate every chain with an explicit default handler, and log or meter the unhandled case if it can still occur.
Keep handlers stateless or request-scoped; a handler shared across requests must not carry per-request state.
Declare the chain from configuration and validate it at startup: required handlers present, order constraints satisfied, no duplicates.
Give each handler one decision — handle and stop, or forward — and document it in the handler's contract; reserve 'do work and always forward' for pipelines where that reading is intended.
Assemble one immutable chain per configuration and reuse it; rebuild only when the policy itself changes.
Test the chain as a unit in addition to the handlers: the order permutations that matter for security and the 'nobody handled it' path.
Name the contract in the type system — a Handler/Middleware interface plus a documented terminal marker — instead of passing around loosely typed callables.

Use async/await uniformly: if the chain is async, every handler must await next() before forwarding; never fire-and-forget the successor call, which causes the chain to stall or return before processing completes.
Add timeout middleware as the outermost or innermost layer to bound latency; a slow or hung handler in the middle otherwise blocks the entire request lifecycle.
Integrate a circuit-breaker per handler for downstream calls: if a handler's dependency is degraded, short-circuit the rest of the chain rather than letting requests queue or fail slowly.
Propagate request-scoped context — tracing IDs, tenant identity, cancellation tokens — explicitly through the chain via a context object, not via shared mutable variables on the handler instance.

Validate the chain composition at startup: check for circular references, verify required handlers are present, and enforce declared ordering constraints (e.g. authentication before authorisation) to catch misconfiguration before production.
When the chain must mutate shared state, use atomic, thread-safe primitives or lock per request; avoid handler-level mutable fields that leak between concurrent requests.
Instrument each handler with metrics (latency, count, error rate) and log entries at chain entry and exit to identify which link is the bottleneck or failure point in production.
Assemble chains via a builder or factory so the chain topology is centralised and testable; never build chains inside handler constructors or handle() methods.
Return the successor reference from set_next() to enable fluent chaining and make the link direction explicit.
Propagate errors instead of swallowing them: translate exceptions into structured responses or re-throw; a handler that silently swallows an error makes debugging the chain near-impossible.
Test each handler in isolation with a mock successor to verify it correctly handles, forwards, or terminates as its contract specifies.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Chain of Responsibility (Behavioral Patterns, Chapter 5).

related_patterns_notes.decorator: Decorator adds behavior around one wrapped object while preserving a continuation contract; Chain of Responsibility may choose a handler and stop without invoking the successor.
related_patterns_notes.composite: Composite forwards through a part/whole object tree; Chain of Responsibility uses an ordered receiver policy, although a parent link can serve as the successor.
related_patterns_notes.command: Command packages a request and its invocation; Chain of Responsibility selects or sequences handlers that may accept that request.
related_patterns_notes.mediator: Mediator centralizes coordination among peers; Chain of Responsibility passes one request serially through potential receivers.
related_patterns_notes.observer: Observer broadcasts an event to subscribers; Chain of Responsibility forwards along an ordered chain and may short-circuit.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Template Method fixes algorithm steps in an inheritance hierarchy; Chain of Responsibility makes receiver membership and order composition data.
related_patterns_notes.interceptor: Interceptor wraps a join point with before/after advice; Chain of Responsibility gives each handler the authority to accept, forward, or stop, although interceptor chains are a common realization.
related_patterns_notes.pipe: Pipe and Filter normally expects each stage to transform and forward a value; Chain of Responsibility permits a link to consume the request or terminate without later stages.
related_patterns_notes.pipeline: Pipeline names an ordered sequence of stages, often all invoked; Chain of Responsibility is defined by the per-link handle/forward/stop decision.
related_patterns_notes.middleware: Middleware is a framework-specific request-pipeline API; Chain of Responsibility is the framework-independent behavioral pattern underneath it.
related_patterns_notes.intercepting-filter: Intercepting Filter specializes the chain for cross-cutting pre/post processing around a target; Chain of Responsibility also covers first-handler-wins event or command dispatch.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: Proxy controls access to one subject; Chain of Responsibility chooses among multiple potential receivers.
